prompt: `Leak` printed `open loans.db` and `use loans.db`, then the exception. Why is there no `close loans.db` line?
hint: Which line of `main` was running when the exception was thrown?

choices.text: The JVM skips `close` when a program is about to end
choices.why: The JVM skips nothing on purpose; line 6 was simply never reached.

choices.text: The exception left `main` at line 5, so line 6 never ran
choices.why: Right: an exception leaves the method at once, and every line after it is skipped.

choices.text: `close` ran, but its output was lost behind the stack trace
choices.why: The trace and the prints share the terminal; a `close` that ran would have printed its line.

choices.text: `Resource` does not implement `AutoCloseable`
choices.why: That matters only for try-with-resources; `Leak` calls `close()` by hand.

prompt: A server catches every exception from a request and moves on to the next one. Each request opens a database connection the way `Leak` opens its resource. What happens over a day?
hint: The process does not end, so nobody takes the connections back.

choices.text: Nothing at all: the garbage collector closes any connection that no variable references any more
choices.why: The garbage collector gives back memory; a connection is held by the database too, and nothing closes it.

choices.text: The server crashes on the first failed request
choices.why: It caught the exception, so it carries on; that is what lets the leak grow.

choices.text: One connection leaks per failure until none are left and requests wait
choices.why: Right: a process that ends hands everything back; a server that runs for days does not.

prompt: `Masked` fails in `use` and then in `close`. What does its stack trace report?
hint: When `finally` throws, its exception replaces the one already on its way out.

choices.text: Only the failure in `close`
choices.why: Right: `use of loans.db failed` is gone, and the trace points at the wrong problem.

choices.text: Only the failure in `use`, because it happened first
choices.why: That is what try-with-resources does; a hand-written `finally` keeps the later one.

choices.text: Both, the second under a line starting with `Suppressed:`
choices.why: `Suppressed:` lines come from try-with-resources, in section 04; `Masked` has none.

choices.text: Neither, because two exceptions at once end the JVM without a message
choices.why: The JVM printed one exception and exit status 1; it was simply the wrong one.

prompt: What did the hand-written `finally` in `Finally.java` cost, compared with the leaking version? Choose all that apply.
hint: Look at where the variable is declared and what a second resource would need.

choices.text: A variable declared outside the `try`, still in scope after the close
choices.why: Yes: `finally` has to see `r`, so `r` lives on after it was closed.

choices.text: Nested `try` blocks as soon as there are two resources
choices.why: Yes: the second must be closed even when closing the first fails.

choices.text: The exception no longer reaching the caller
choices.why: It still reached the caller; the trace after `close loans.db` shows it.

choices.text: A slower program, because `finally` runs on a separate thread
choices.why: `finally` runs on the same thread, right after the `try` block is left.

prompt: Why does the garbage collector not solve the problem of section 02?
hint: What does it give back?

choices.text: It does not run while an exception is being thrown
choices.why: It runs whenever the JVM decides; the trouble is what it gives back, not when.

choices.text: It gives back memory and nothing else
choices.why: Right: an open file or a connection is held outside the program's memory.

choices.text: It only collects objects created with `new`
choices.why: Every object is created with `new`, the resource included.

prompt: What must a class do for its objects to be declared in a try-with-resources?
hint: `StringBuilder` was refused, and so would the first `Resource` have been.

choices.text: Have a public method called `close`
choices.why: The first `Resource` had one and would still be refused; the rule is the interface.

choices.text: Hold something that is not memory
choices.why: The compiler cannot see what a class holds; it checks the type.

choices.text: Implement `AutoCloseable`
choices.why: Right: one interface with one method, `close()`, and the compiler checks it.

choices.text: Be declared `final` so it cannot be swapped inside the block
choices.why: The resource variable is implicitly final; the class itself need not be.

prompt: `Order` opens `loans.db`, then `audit.log`, and the body throws. Put what happened in order.
hint: Reverse order for the closes, and the handlers come after them.
items: the `catch` prints `caught: use of audit.log failed`

prompt: A writer is built on top of a file, and both are declared in one try-with-resources, the file first. Why does closing in reverse order matter here?
hint: Which one depends on the other?

choices.text: It does not: the order is alphabetical by variable name
choices.why: `audit.log` closed before `loans.db` because it was opened second, not because of its name.

choices.text: The writer flushes into the file while it closes, so the file has to be open then
choices.why: Right: the later resource depends on the earlier one, and reverse order never pulls the floor out from under it.

choices.text: Closing the file first would make the compiler refuse the block
choices.why: The order is fixed by the language; there is nothing for the compiler to refuse.

prompt: Inside the `catch` of `Order`, can the handler still call `db.use(false)`?
hint: Where does the variable `db` exist, and when was it closed?

choices.text: Yes, because the resource is closed only after the `catch` block and the `finally` have both finished
choices.why: The output says otherwise: both closes printed before `caught:`.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the class is marked with `@Override`
choices.why: `@Override` marks a method, and it has nothing to do with scope.

choices.text: No: `db` exists only inside the `try` block, and it is already closed
choices.why: Right: the compiler refuses the name, and the object behind it was given back.

prompt: `java CountLines missing.txt` threw `NoSuchFileException`. Which `close` ran?
hint: Did the reader ever exist?

choices.text: None: the reader's initialiser threw, so there was nothing to close
choices.why: Right: try-with-resources closes only what was actually opened.

choices.text: The reader's, with a `null` that was then ignored
choices.why: No `close` is called on a resource that was never assigned; there is no `null` to ignore.

choices.text: The reader's, and its exception was suppressed into the `NoSuchFileException` that reached `main`
choices.why: A suppressed exception would have printed a `Suppressed:` line; there was none.

choices.text: The file system's own, inside `Files.newBufferedReader`
choices.why: Nothing was opened, so the JDK's methods had nothing to close either.

prompt: `BufferedReader`, files, sockets and database connections qualify for try-with-resources because they implement `AutoCloseable`, most of them through the older sub-interface `java.io.___`.
hint: It has the same method and an older name.

prompt: `javac NotCloseable.java` refused `try (StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder())`. Why?
hint: Read the second line of the error.

choices.text: A `StringBuilder` cannot be created inside parentheses
choices.why: Any expression can initialise a resource; the type is what was refused.

choices.text: `StringBuilder` cannot be converted to `AutoCloseable`
choices.why: Right: it holds only memory and has no `close`, and the compiler says so.

choices.text: The block has no `catch` clause, and a resource declared in parentheses needs one to compile
choices.why: `Twr` had no `catch` and compiled; `catch` is optional.

prompt: In try-with-resources, the body throws and then `close` throws. Which exception reaches the caller?
hint: The opposite of `Masked`.

choices.text: The one from `close`, because it happened last
choices.why: That is the hand-written `finally` of section 02, which lost the cause.

choices.text: A new exception that wraps both of them, with the body's failure as its cause
choices.why: No new exception is made; the body's is kept and the other is attached to it.

choices.text: The body's, carrying the one from `close` as suppressed
choices.why: Right: the cause is what you read first, and the close failure is still in the report.

prompt: Every `Throwable` returns its suppressed exceptions as an array from the method `___()`.
hint: `Inspect` looped over it.

prompt: `Inspect` printed `suppressed: close of audit.log failed` before `suppressed: close of loans.db failed`. Why that order?
hint: They are added as the closes happen.

choices.text: Suppressed exceptions are sorted alphabetically by their message text
choices.why: No sorting happens; the list is in the order the failures were added.

choices.text: `audit.log` was opened second, so it was closed, and failed, first
choices.why: Right: the closes run in reverse order and each failure is added as it happens.

choices.text: The array is filled from its end, so the newest is first
choices.why: The newest is last; `audit.log`'s failure is simply the older one.

choices.text: `getSuppressed` returns the order the resources were declared, reversed for safety
choices.why: It returns the order of addition; the reversal comes from the closing order, not from the method.

prompt: The `close` failure was at `Resource.java:22` in `Masked` and at `Resource.java:23` in `Suppressed`, though the throw statement is the same. Why?
hint: Which `Resource.java` was compiled each time?

choices.text: The suppressed trace counts lines from one instead of from zero
choices.why: Both traces count from one; the files were different.

choices.text: try-with-resources adds a hidden line to `Resource`, which pushes every later line down by one
choices.why: The generated code lives in the calling class, not in `Resource`; its line numbers are untouched.

choices.text: The second file has an extra `@Override` line above `close`
choices.why: Right: a stack trace numbers the lines of the file that was compiled.

prompt: In try-with-resources, match what failed to what the caller receives.
hint: The table at the end of section 04.

pairs.right: the body's exception, with the close's suppressed in it

right_distractors: the exception from `close`, with the body's as its cause

prompt: A method opens a file in try-with-resources and returns from inside the block. Before the caller receives the value, what has happened to the file?
hint: The generated code is a `finally`, and lesson 36 said when `finally` runs.

choices.text: It was closed, because leaving the block by `return` still closes the resource
choices.why: Right: every way out of the block closes it, a `return` included.

choices.text: It stays open until the garbage collector finds the unreachable reader
choices.why: That would be the leak; the block closes it on the way out.

choices.text: It stays open, because `return` skips the generated close
choices.why: `return` does not skip a `finally`, and try-with-resources is one.

choices.text: The compiler refuses a `return` inside try-with-resources
choices.why: Returning from inside the block is ordinary and compiles.

prompt: You review code with `try { conn = open(); ... } finally { conn.close(); }`. What is the strongest reason to rewrite it with try-with-resources?
hint: Think of the day both the work and the close fail.

choices.text: try-with-resources runs faster, because it skips the generated `finally` code
choices.why: Both compile to much the same code; speed is not the argument.

choices.text: A `finally` block is deprecated since Java 7, the release in which try-with-resources replaced it
choices.why: `finally` is alive and well; try-with-resources is built from one.

choices.text: Its original exception survives when `close` fails too
choices.why: Right: the hand-written version reports the close failure and loses the cause.

prompt: A try-with-resources declares three resources. All three open, the body throws, and every `close` throws too. How many suppressed exceptions does the body's exception carry?
hint: One per failed close.
